power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: MEADOWS was another large trial (19) examining Memantine vs placebo for cognitive decline. Despite a relatively short 1-year recruitment window, and restricting inclusion to adults with DS aged >40 and/or with dementia, 173 were successfully randomised (96.11% of the 180 target). Authors described premature closure of the recruitment window (once 173 of the target 180 participants were randomised) due to a 'funding constraint' preventing them from achieving their target. Recruitment was via four learning disability centres in the UK and Norway. 254 people were assessed for eligibility, suggesting good conversion of eligible to recruited participants. The trial had broad inclusion criteria permitting participation irrespective of dementia diagnosis, which may also have aided recruitment. Participants were eligible if they were residents in a care facility or had a carer willing to help ensure compliance, also likely contributing to low attrition (16%; n=146) at primary outcome (52 weeks). Participants were also permitted to decline some study visits without withdrawing from the trial. Altogether, high recruitment and low attrition rates were achieved, and failure to reach the target sample minimally reduced power from 91% to 90%.

text.text: Background: Adults with Down Syndrome (DS) face significant health inequalities.
Evidence from high-quality randomised controlled trials (RCTs) for interventions are lacking, and there is a perceived difficulty regarding recruiting and retaining participants with DS.
Aims: This systematic review aimed to examine planned vs. actual recruitment and retention rates of RCTs involving adults with DS, summarising reported facilitators of and barriers to participation.

Method: MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and EMBASE databases were searched systematically to retrieve RCTs of any intervention involving adults with DS =>16yrs, published to 07/12/2023, with a second search in April 2025.

Trial design, planned and achieved sample size, retention rate, and recruitment and retention strategies were extracted

text.text: This methodological field-wide review therefore examines the types of interventions evaluated in RCTs involving adults with DS, as well as recruitment and retention rates, and barriers and facilitators to participation.

The findings will help clinicians and researchers in designing more accessible and effective RCTs for this population, and improving future trial methodology that ultimately contributes to their health and wellbeing.
The objectives were: 1.
Compare planned versus actual recruitment and attrition rates; 2.
Explore barriers to trial participation; 3.
Identify strategies used to improve access and participation.
This review was prospectively registered on Prospero on September 4 th 2023 (CRD42023447126).

text.text: Post deduplication, 1,622 articles underwent title and abstract screening, of which 89 full texts were reviewed for eligibility.
Five additional studies were identified from reviewing reference lists.

A further 16 were identified from registry reviews, but were excluded (8 due to not meeting inclusion criteria; 6 reflected registrations of trials already identified from database searches, and 2 reflected ongoing trials, for which recruitment and retention data were therefore not available). 66 papers were included in the final analysis, reflecting 44 completed trials (n.b., some trials were represented by multiple papers e.g., papers describing the trial protocol, pilot trial, and fullscale RCT).
The most common recruitment countries were the USA (n=14 RCTs, 31.82%) and Spain (n=7 RCTs, 15.91%).

Areas of research included improving physical fitness (n=18 RCTs, 40.91%), dementia/cognitive impairment treatment or prevention (n=12 RCTs, 27.27%), and improving cognitive/neuropsychological function (n=7 RCTs, 15.91%).
The most frequently trialled interventions included exercise programmes (n=20 RCTs, 45.5%) and medications (n=18 RCTs, 40.91%).
Primary outcome timepoints ranged from several hours to up to 3 years (median = 12 weeks; see Table 1 and Supplemental Materials Table 3 for a comprehensive summary of trial characteristics).

text.text: The 44 completed RCTs included in this review randomised a total of 1,785 individuals.
Just 13 studies (29.50%) were prospectively registered in accessible trial registries, and only 4 trials (9.09%) had a pre-published protocol.

Evidence of a pre-specified target sample size reported in either a pre-published protocol, trial registry, or in the trial results publication was unavailable for most trials (n=16, 36.36%), with most not reporting a power calculation (n=12, 27.27%).

It was not possible to categorise the majority of reported trials as either full-scale or pilot/feasibility trials (unclear n=23, 52.27%), with 12 categorised as pilot/feasibility (27.27%), and 9 categorised as full-scale trials (20.45%).
There was large variation in recruited sample sizes, with most recruiting small Ns.
Just 13 of the included studies recruited a total N ≥40 (29.55%; range of all studies = 8-337, median N=25, IQR 21.75).

text.text: The largest trial explored vitamin E supplementation in adults with DS aged 50+, recruiting participants over an 8 year period (18).
text.formatted: The largest trial explored vitamin E supplementation in adults with DS aged 50+, recruiting participants over an 8 year period <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: An international consortium of 21 experienced clinical sites across 5 countries aimed to recruit 400 participants. 349 people were screened, with 337 randomised (84.25% of the target sample).
The authors aimed to include as many participants aged >40 as possible.
text.formatted: The authors aimed to include as many participants aged >40 as possible.

text.text: To achieve this, they did not exclude individuals based on severity of ID or for having dementia (common exclusion criteria in other studies).
To address concerns about the target population's "high likelihood of limited decision-making capacity", the study engaged families and legally authorised representatives.
Other strategies to minimise burden included avoiding collecting blood biomarkers where possible, and shortening cognitive tests.
Family members or carers were also designated as 'study partners' and were key in supervising medication adherence.
Overall, 274 individuals were retained over 36 months of follow-up (attrition 19%).
MEADOWS was another large trial (19) examining Memantine vs placebo for cognitive decline.
text.formatted: MEADOWS was another large trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref> examining Memantine vs placebo for cognitive decline.

text.text: Despite a relatively short 1-year recruitment window, and restricting inclusion to adults with DS aged >40 and/or with dementia, 173 were successfully randomised (96.11% of the 180 target).
text.formatted: Despite a relatively short 1-year recruitment window, and restricting inclusion to adults with DS aged >40 and/or with dementia, 173 were successfully randomised (96.11% of the 180 target).

text.text: Authors described premature closure of the recruitment window (once 173 of the target 180 participants were randomised) due to a 'funding constraint' preventing them from achieving their target.
Recruitment was via four learning disability centres in the UK and Norway. 254 people were assessed for eligibility, suggesting good conversion of eligible to recruited participants.
The trial had broad inclusion criteria permitting participation irrespective of dementia diagnosis, which may also have aided recruitment.

Participants were eligible if they were residents in a care facility or had a carer willing to help ensure compliance, also likely contributing to low attrition (16%; n=146) at primary outcome (52 weeks).
Participants were also permitted to decline some study visits without withdrawing from the trial.
Altogether, high recruitment and low attrition rates were achieved, and failure to reach the target sample minimally reduced power from 91% to 90%.

The third largest trial (20) explored the effect of Donepezil on Severe Impairment Battery scores (neuropsychological evaluation of cognitive function) for young adults with DS. 123 of the N=160 target sample were recruited from 24 centres experienced in working with this population across the USA.

Despite this, and a 3-year recruitment period, authors described premature closure of recruitment due to 'slow individual enrolment', attributing this to feedback from those declining participation that they had reached a period of "relative stability" in their lives at ages 18-35 and did not want to disrupt this by participating.
However, just 7% of participants were lost to follow-up, with 115 completing primary outcome at 12 weeks.
The largest pilot trial identified was conducted at two secondary care sites and explored antioxidant supplementation in adults with DS and dementia (21).
text.formatted: The largest pilot trial identified was conducted at two secondary care sites and explored antioxidant supplementation in adults with DS and dementia <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref>.

text.text: Of 73 people screened, 59 were eligible and 58 randomised.

Primary outcomes were assessed at 2 years for 31 people (47% attrition), a higher rate than expected, but reported by the authors to be in line with dementia trials in the general population (22, 23).
text.formatted: Primary outcomes were assessed at 2 years for 31 people (47% attrition), a higher rate than expected, but reported by the authors to be in line with dementia trials in the general population <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23)</ref>.

text.text: They compared this high attrition rate to a much lower rate in a trial of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in those with Alzheimer's without DS (24), a much larger trial (N=686) which may have achieved better retention due to recruitment of those with mild-moderate dementia, compared to those with more severe dementia here (21).
text.formatted: They compared this high attrition rate to a much lower rate in a trial of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in those with Alzheimer's without DS <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref>, a much larger trial (N=686) which may have achieved better retention due to recruitment of those with mild-moderate dementia, compared to those with more severe dementia here <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref>.

text.text: Given reasons for attrition before 2-year follow-up included refusal to participate (n=9), use of non-permitted concomitant medications (n=3), and death (n=2).
Of those retained, supplement adherence was high (90.4% placebo, 91.9% antioxidant); above the 70% rate required for efficacy analyses.
On the whole, included studies did not provide much detail regarding their participant recruitment methods and associated challenges.
However, some trials described recruitment difficulties, which could be broadly divided into concerns related to study design, and those attributable to participant-level factors:
Design factors included sampling method, recruitment site, inclusion criteria, and delays in obtaining ethical approval.
For example, Cooper et al. (2016) recruited via community sources, Down Syndrome Scotland, Local Authorities, and Scottish NHS services.
Researchers made significant efforts during the yearlong recruitment period to meet with managers of local support organisations, but found that this did not translate to recruitment.
Instead, most participants were recruited from health professionals and day services, particularly via a national primary care research network.

The authors described recruitment as highly labourintensive, particularly contacting each primary care practice in the network, whereby many declined to assist due to a perception that their service would have too few eligible participants.

The trial team suggested that future RCTs should make clear that although each service may have only a few potential participants, their input is crucial in facilitating recruitment from as many sources as possible.

Similarly, authors were optimistic that the adoption of remote access to general practice records could streamline this process, targeting resources to specific practices more likely to have multiple eligible participants (25).
text.formatted: Similarly, authors were optimistic that the adoption of remote access to general practice records could streamline this process, targeting resources to specific practices more likely to have multiple eligible participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>.

text.text: Recruitment methods varied significantly between trials, often due in part to the varying nature of the interventions themselves (e.g., recruitment for surgical or medication trials is naturally different to recruitment for exercise interventions).
Enrolling successive patients referred to an anaesthetic service over a 24-month period for surgical trial (26) was described as "challenging and time-consuming".

Other methods used across included studies were recruiting from community support groups for people with DS and ID (27), residential facilities (28) (29) (30), or special education schools (15), which, while limiting sample size, often produced lower attrition rates (0-9%).
text.formatted: Other methods used across included studies were recruiting from community support groups for people with DS and ID <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref>, residential facilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref>, or special education schools (15), which, while limiting sample size, often produced lower attrition rates (0-9%).

text.text: Relatedly, reported barriers to retention were often context-specific, including patients not attending inperson appointments due to concerns about catching Covid-19 (31).
text.formatted: Relatedly, reported barriers to retention were often context-specific, including patients not attending inperson appointments due to concerns about catching Covid-19 <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref>.

text.text: The same study also described abandonment of a secondary outcome cognitive test as completion took too long, highlighting the need to ensure tests are appropriate for this population (31).
text.formatted: The same study also described abandonment of a secondary outcome cognitive test as completion took too long, highlighting the need to ensure tests are appropriate for this population <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref>.

text.text: The TOP-COG trial described barriers inherent to trials assessing treatments for cognitive decline (25); inclusion criteria were restricted to adults with DS aged ³50 years, in an attempt to keep inclusion broad enough to facilitate recruitment, but also limiting the length of the trial period during which cognitive decline would likely be seen.
text.formatted: The TOP-COG trial described barriers inherent to trials assessing treatments for cognitive decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>; inclusion criteria were restricted to adults with DS aged ³50 years, in an attempt to keep inclusion broad enough to facilitate recruitment, but also limiting the length of the trial period during which cognitive decline would likely be seen.

text.text: The authors explained that altering the inclusion criteria to include those aged 40-45 may have meant that a longer follow-up period was required (and associated funding/resources).
Similarly, longer follow-up could further reduce retention, affecting statistical power.

The TESDAD trial (32) also described sub-optimal concordance with a cognitive training programme, with an average of 1.9 out of 3 sessions completed per week, but were able to retain 84 of their 87 participants (96.6%) at 52 weeks.
The highly demanding nature of the intervention may explain in part why the trial design was later adapted (i.e., widening of inclusion criteria).
Delays in ethical approval also posed a recruitment barrier for at least one trial.

A trial of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for obstructive sleep apnoea (33) initially showed promise as a large recruiter, with invitations sent to over 5,000 adults with DS who had been involved in a prior related trial (34). 97 respondents were eligible.
text.formatted: A trial of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for obstructive sleep apnoea (33) initially showed promise as a large recruiter, with invitations sent to over 5,000 adults with DS who had been involved in a prior related trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(34)</ref>. 97 respondents were eligible.

text.text: However, only 28 (28.9%) were enrolled due to 'unacceptable delays in ethical approval', which delayed the trial team's ability to contact potential participants, and resulted in funding running out, despite a short treatment window of 4 weeks.

Participant-level factors impacting recruitment included demographics (e.g., age, employment status, living arrangements, dementia diagnosis status), participant awareness about health concerns, and concerns about research and trial processes.
For example, multiple studies reported difficulty recruiting younger participants.

Similar to concerns about disrupting a period of relative stability (20), in a study evaluating a fitness and health education programme (14) which initially successfully recruited 89 people, almost one-third (n=28, 31.5%) withdrew consent before randomisation, with the most common reason being conflict with work schedules.
text.formatted: Similar to concerns about disrupting a period of relative stability <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20)</ref>, in a study evaluating a fitness and health education programme (14) which initially successfully recruited 89 people, almost one-third (n=28, 31.5%) withdrew consent before randomisation, with the most common reason being conflict with work schedules.

text.text: This clash between work and trial participation may be further compounded by the time of day of interventions, and scheduling inflexibility, e.g., evening fitness programme sessions may be more compatible with a standard working/volunteering day.
Severe ID was also indirectly discussed by some as a potential barrier to recruitment.
Concerns regarding ethicality, and the logistics of obtaining consent were common.

Strategies to overcome this included taking an individualised approach to consent, such that degree of ID was not an exclusion criterion per se (35), with capacity to consent instead being evaluated on a case by case basis by clinicians.
text.formatted: Strategies to overcome this included taking an individualised approach to consent, such that degree of ID was not an exclusion criterion per se <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(35)</ref>, with capacity to consent instead being evaluated on a case by case basis by clinicians.

text.text: In addition, several studies obtained consent from legal guardians when participants were unable to consent for themselves (36, 37), and in some cases also demonstrated how carers and family could be involved in the research process beyond consent retrieval (38), e.g., playing a role as facilitators for participant concordance with physical activity or medication adherence.

text.text: Study teams emphasised the importance of targeting both participants and their parents/carers in the recruitment process.
A further participant factor explored was awareness of the health issues and inequalities faced by people with DS.

A study of statin therapy and cognition in ageing adults with DS identified a lack of awareness around the risk of Alzheimer's dementia for this population (25), negatively impacting desire to participate.
text.formatted: A study of statin therapy and cognition in ageing adults with DS identified a lack of awareness around the risk of Alzheimer's dementia for this population <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>, negatively impacting desire to participate.

text.text: Lack of understanding about trial processes was also reported as a potential barrier to recruitment.

In one study of a cycling intervention, authors described difficulty recruiting due to potential participants' guardians having a clear preference for the active intervention (motor-assisted cycling vs. no cycling (problem of equipoise; (39)).
text.formatted: In one study of a cycling intervention, authors described difficulty recruiting due to potential participants' guardians having a clear preference for the active intervention (motor-assisted cycling vs. no cycling (problem of equipoise; <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(39)</ref>).

text.text: Therefore, researchers decided to adapt the control group and instead compare self-paced with motor-assisted cycling to aid recruitment, but with the potential of limiting the likelihood of finding a difference between groups.

Some studies reported reasons given by those declining to participate, including not wanting to take medication outside of the need to "treat" a condition, rather than for prevention, and also managing uncertainty about RCT processes, such as blinding and randomisation (25).
text.formatted: Some studies reported reasons given by those declining to participate, including not wanting to take medication outside of the need to "treat" a condition, rather than for prevention, and also managing uncertainty about RCT processes, such as blinding and randomisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>.

text.text: Difficulty was also reported in recruiting people from underrepresented ethnic groups (31), though none of the included studies described strategies to ameliorate this.
text.formatted: Difficulty was also reported in recruiting people from underrepresented ethnic groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref>, though none of the included studies described strategies to ameliorate this.

text.text: In a pilot RCT of Donepezil versus placebo for adults with DS and Alzheimer's (40), authors identified that the recruitment target would not be achieved unless significant methodological changes were made (e.g., broadening inclusion criteria and expanding recruitment sites).
text.formatted: In a pilot RCT of Donepezil versus placebo for adults with DS and Alzheimer's <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(40)</ref>, authors identified that the recruitment target would not be achieved unless significant methodological changes were made (e.g., broadening inclusion criteria and expanding recruitment sites).

text.text: However, although it was known that the trial would be underpowered, it was continued (recruited: n=31, retained: n=27 by 24 weeks).
Other trials described modifying their design to facilitate participation.

For example, the TESDAD trial (41) explored the safety and tolerability of dietary supplementation with Epigallocetachin-3-gallate (EGCG), or placebo plus cognitive training to improve cognitive abilities.

The authors described initial difficulty recruiting from outpatient settings across the Catalan Down Syndrome Association, and so the eligible age range was widened (from 18-30 to 16-34yrs; recruited n=87, retained: n=84; 96.6% to primary outcome at 52 weeks).

Strategies were also incorporated in study design to maximise retention, including using a crossover or delayed intervention (42) as these were felt to increase the likelihood that control group participants would be retained, as they knew they would receive the intervention later.

Recruiting from lists of past study participants also proved effective for some (43), resulting in higher eligibility rates (as participants had effectively been pre-screened in previous trials), and may also promote retention, as participants were highly motivated, already known to be able to tolerate similar interventions, and may have developed good relationships with study teams.
text.formatted: Recruiting from lists of past study participants also proved effective for some <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(43)</ref>, resulting in higher eligibility rates (as participants had effectively been pre-screened in previous trials), and may also promote retention, as participants were highly motivated, already known to be able to tolerate similar interventions, and may have developed good relationships with study teams.

text.text: In other trials however, benefits of recruiting past participants were more modest ((44): 74 people contacted; 26 assessed for eligibility; 16 randomised).
Many strategies to promote participation centred around two themes of maximising participant convenience and minimising burden.
Carer-participant dyads in the TOP-COG study expressed a preference for "unobtrusive" trials which do not "impact (my) daily life" (25).
text.formatted: Carer-participant dyads in the TOP-COG study expressed a preference for "unobtrusive" trials which do not "impact (my) daily life" <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>.

text.text: Participant convenience was maximised in several studies by offering home visits or online appointments (25, 45), which in some cases also inadvertently increased the accuracy of cognitive measures, with participants able to complete these in their familiar home setting. Shields et al. (2008) also achieved 0% attrition of their 20 participants (and 92.8% concordance with the intervention) at 10 weeks via several strategies to minimise participant burden, including providing transport to the exercise intervention, and limiting the intervention period to 10 weeks (46).

(2008)</ref> also achieved 0% attrition of their 20 participants (and 92.8% concordance with the intervention) at 10 weeks via several strategies to minimise participant burden, including providing transport to the exercise intervention, and limiting the intervention period to 10 weeks <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(46)</ref>.

text.text: Other studies also described shortening intervention duration or frequency of sessions (e.g., exercise interventions (47)), to boost intervention concordance and sustainability of behaviour change.
Shorter intervention periods may also boost study retention.

For example, the low attrition rate (8%, n=37) at 16 weeks seen in a trial of NMDA-antagonism for cognition in 40 young adults with DS (a demographically challenging group to recruit and retain (35)), may be at least in part attributable to the short 16-week trial duration.
Other factors such as involvement of carers/family to support concordance (e.g., overseeing medication administration) may also contribute.

In a pilot trial exploring the effect of NMDA antagonism on cognitive function in young adults with DS, a short form version of a cognitive test was used after the first enrolled participant could not complete the outcome measure 'in a timely manner' (35).

text.text: Another exercise intervention trial described considerations made to avoid potential issues with physical discomfort and injuries specific to individuals with ID, including a physical examination conducted pre-participation to rule out underlying disease that could affect physical performance (47).
text.formatted: Another exercise intervention trial described considerations made to avoid potential issues with physical discomfort and injuries specific to individuals with ID, including a physical examination conducted pre-participation to rule out underlying disease that could affect physical performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(47)</ref>.

text.text: The trial team also incorporated fewer exercise sessions per week than is usually for such studies (3 instead of 5), over a relatively longer period (10 weeks) to improve compliance (47).
text.formatted: The trial team also incorporated fewer exercise sessions per week than is usually for such studies (3 instead of 5), over a relatively longer period (10 weeks) to improve compliance <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(47)</ref>.

text.text: Another exercise intervention trial conducted sessions in the mornings, due to an understanding that people with ID tend to be less active in afternoons and evenings, achieving 100% retention of 36 participants over 12 weeks and 96% adherence (37).

text.text: Further exercise studies described varying class intensity/task to maintain engagement (48).
text.formatted: Further exercise studies described varying class intensity/task to maintain engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(48)</ref>.

text.text: Trial teams also recognised that invasive procedures such as blood tests can be particularly aversive for people with ID (37, 49), deciding to only taking one blood sample at a timepoint most likely to detect a change (37).

text.text: Other exercise intervention trials often considered that people with DS may require adapted interventions due to vulnerability to injury (38) caused by physiological differences such as joint hypermobility, hypotonia, and chronotropic incompetence (16, 50).

text.text: Common comorbidities such as congenital heart abnormalities were also perceived as too high-risk, and so were often applied as exclusion criteria (39), further reducing the pool of eligible participants.
text.formatted: Common comorbidities such as congenital heart abnormalities were also perceived as too high-risk, and so were often applied as exclusion criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(39)</ref>, further reducing the pool of eligible participants.

text.text: However, despite concern regarding injuries, no studies reported sport injury-related reasons for participant drop out.
This may therefore reflect a discordance between researcher and participant concerns.

Indeed, Heller The study also used a sticker book to log sessions attended, and participants met with a researcher 2-3 times per week to discuss and ameliorate any participation barriers (e.g., offering an alternative if a particular exercise was not enjoyed/too challenging) (42).

text.text: Another key strategy to maximise participation was providing incentives or motivation.
One trial sent motivational postcard reminders (44) and provided reimbursement for travel expenses (44), with a compliance rate of 96%.
text.formatted: One trial sent motivational postcard reminders (44) and provided reimbursement for travel expenses <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(44)</ref>, with a compliance rate of 96%.

text.text: Other incentives included weekly virtual meetings with health educators, allowing participants to keep a FitBit (fitness smart watch), and a $25 payment at the beginning and end of the trial, with no attrition of their 27 participants and 83.5-89.5% concordance with the exercise intervention (45).

text.text: Another study also achieved 0% attrition (primary outcome at 56±14 days post-baseline), having selected a motivated cohort of people who had been involved in previous research, shortening assessment tools, and allowing participants to choose the design of their eye-glasses as part of the study (43).

text.text: The relational aspects of participation were also thought to be important for retention.
Encouragement provided by research teams at weekly meetings (44) or during exercise sessions (36,50) were found to improve retention and increase participant satisfaction.
One study even held an awards ceremony at the end of participation to celebrate participants' achievements (14), which may also have incentivised retention.
text.formatted: One study even held an awards ceremony at the end of participation to celebrate participants' achievements <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>, which may also have incentivised retention.

text.text: Finally, participant-carer dyads in the TOP-COG study reported gratitude to researchers for home visits ("it was nice for you to come and visit us") and providing emotional support ("I've unloaded on you… you've been a good sounding board") (25).

text.text: One RCT exploring an adapted group cycling intervention for self-efficacy (50) also discussed peer-support as a motivational tool, with one parent of a participant describing a "comradery" between participants, with interpersonal dynamics encouraging her son's participation.
This systematic review examined the recruitment and retention strategies employed by 44 RCTs involving adults with DS.

We identified a predominance of small-scale trials, with variable reporting practices both before and after the implementation of CONSORT guidelines (51), with very few included studies providing target sample sizes, power calculations, or pre-registered protocols.
text.formatted: We identified a predominance of small-scale trials, with variable reporting practices both before and after the implementation of CONSORT guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(51)</ref>, with very few included studies providing target sample sizes, power calculations, or pre-registered protocols.

text.text: Recruitment appeared to be difficult, although regular omission of target Ns made calculating recruitment success challenging.
Retention was also variable between trials.
Only one third of the included trials recruited N ≥40 in total (i.e., 20 per arm in a standard two-arm RCT).
Some trials reported strategies to minimise participant burden and provided incentives to maximise recruitment and minimise attrition.

The most successful trials capitalised on multicentre collaboration and reaching established participant networks at experienced centres (52), which may go some way to addressing recruitment challenges when conducting research with people with rare conditions.
text.formatted: The most successful trials capitalised on multicentre collaboration and reaching established participant networks at experienced centres <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(52)</ref>, which may go some way to addressing recruitment challenges when conducting research with people with rare conditions.

text.text: In designing the trials, they also adapted interventions and assessments to reduce study burden and facilitate engagement, and involved family or carers throughout participation.
The findings are discussed in turn below.

Prasher et al. (2002) described inherent challenges associated with recruiting people with ID to trials, including the relative rarity of the condition, such that the potentially recruitable population is small, and the likelihood of reaching recruitment goals for sufficient statistical power is therefore reduced.
text.formatted: Prasher et al. <ref type="bibr">(2002)</ref> described inherent challenges associated with recruiting people with ID to trials, including the relative rarity of the condition, such that the potentially recruitable population is small, and the likelihood of reaching recruitment goals for sufficient statistical power is therefore reduced.

text.text: This challenge was reflected in the included studies, e.g., with few eligible participants with DS in primary care (53), or <10% of residents at a specialist ID centre having DS (54).
text.formatted: This challenge was reflected in the included studies, e.g., with few eligible participants with DS in primary care <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(53)</ref>, or <10% of residents at a specialist ID centre having DS <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(54)</ref>.

text.text: The relatively high incidence of comorbidity associated with DS, including obstructive sleep apnoea, leukaemia, metabolic syndrome, epilepsy, ASD, and Alzheimer's dementia (2-5) can also further limit the number of eligible participants depending on how stringent studyspecific exclusion criteria are.
For example, those with Alzheimer's were often excluded, despite high prevalence in the ageing DS population.
Some studies described attempts to address this, including making live changes to trial inclusion criteria (41) and targeting recruitment from previous participant pools (43, 44).
text.formatted: Some studies described attempts to address this, including making live changes to trial inclusion criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(41)</ref> and targeting recruitment from previous participant pools <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44)</ref>.

text.text: Difficulties gaining ethical approval represent a further challenge to trials with ID populations, primarily due to concerns about obtaining informed consent.

In one study (40), obtaining approval took over a year due e.g., to the perceived vulnerability of the population and their difficulty providing consent, or potentially reduced ability to recognise, interpret, or communicate internal experiences.
text.formatted: In one study <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(40)</ref>, obtaining approval took over a year due e.g., to the perceived vulnerability of the population and their difficulty providing consent, or potentially reduced ability to recognise, interpret, or communicate internal experiences.

text.text: The TOP-COG study also discussed such concerns during nested qualitative interviews with participants and carers; e.g., a carer voiced fears that research processes may take advantage of or 'use' people with DS, exploiting perceived vulnerability when testing a drug that they worried "could be harmful" (25).
text.formatted: The TOP-COG study also discussed such concerns during nested qualitative interviews with participants and carers; e.g., a carer voiced fears that research processes may take advantage of or 'use' people with DS, exploiting perceived vulnerability when testing a drug that they worried "could be harmful" <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>.

text.text: A similar exploration of parent attitudes towards clinical trials of cognition-enhancing treatments highlighted a reluctance to allow their children to take part for fear of altering their personality, or risking new mental health concerns as a result of cognitive improvements without corresponding improvements to medical/physical impairments (55).
text.formatted: A similar exploration of parent attitudes towards clinical trials of cognition-enhancing treatments highlighted a reluctance to allow their children to take part for fear of altering their personality, or risking new mental health concerns as a result of cognitive improvements without corresponding improvements to medical/physical impairments <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(55)</ref>.

text.text: Parents wished for researchers to use the priorities of individuals with DS and their families to inform their work (see e.g., Lim et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Parents wished for researchers to use the priorities of individuals with DS and their families to inform their work (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Lim et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, protecting vulnerable populations must be balanced with respect for individual autonomy and the right to selfdetermination (52), e.g., in deciding to participate in a trial.

TOP-COG and other studies highlight the importance of careful communication with participants and carers to address concerns and dispel misconceptions, recognising the important role family and carers play in facilitating study engagement.
Although research shows that most people with DS have paid carers, yet there is no clear guidance on how best to involve carers and family members in trials (57).
text.formatted: Although research shows that most people with DS have paid carers, yet there is no clear guidance on how best to involve carers and family members in trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(57)</ref>.

text.text: Novel methods of obtaining informed consent, such as picture-based or electronic consenting methods have also been discussed (52).
text.formatted: Novel methods of obtaining informed consent, such as picture-based or electronic consenting methods have also been discussed <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(52)</ref>.

text.text: However, none of the included studies reported employing such methods, perhaps reflecting concerns about ethical implications.
Individuals with DS are a highly heterogenous group, making study design and selection of outcome measures challenging.
Validated DS-specific instruments are only recently emerging (58, 59), and ceiling or floor effects of existing tools are demonstrated in the included trials (18).
text.formatted: Validated DS-specific instruments are only recently emerging <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59)</ref>, and ceiling or floor effects of existing tools are demonstrated in the included trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Trials in this review largely employed self-report, subjective assessment tools, which may also be particularly susceptible to placebo effects (52).
text.formatted: Trials in this review largely employed self-report, subjective assessment tools, which may also be particularly susceptible to placebo effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(52)</ref>.

text.text: Equally, heterogeneity in outcomes may lead to a greater likelihood of trials prematurely concluding that treatments offer no benefit, when there may be a clear benefit for a distinct subgroup (52).
text.formatted: Equally, heterogeneity in outcomes may lead to a greater likelihood of trials prematurely concluding that treatments offer no benefit, when there may be a clear benefit for a distinct subgroup <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(52)</ref>.

text.text: However, some studies discussed initial attempts to adapt outcome measures and interventions after participant feedback, as well as based on assumptions about people with DS (35, 37, 47), showing initial promise for the application of co-production methods in RCTs with adults with DS (42).
text.formatted: However, some studies discussed initial attempts to adapt outcome measures and interventions after participant feedback, as well as based on assumptions about people with DS <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47)</ref>, showing initial promise for the application of co-production methods in RCTs with adults with DS <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(42)</ref>.

text.text: It should however be noted that, wherever possible, trial teams should engage with individuals with DS and their families at the earliest opportunity (i.e., during protocol design) to ensure that accessible protocols are co-produced prior to trial commencement, after which amendments to trial interventions and outcome measures are usually not permitted.

Although trial teams should consider focusing on quality of the recruitment as represented by engaged, wellinformed, consenting participants, retained for the study duration (60), studies not recruiting to their target sample size, nor recruiting a sufficiently large sample (i.e., N ≥40 as a minimum), are at risk of compromising external validity.

text.text: Public health communications should also make clear the necessity of RCT processes, such as blinding and randomisation (5, 25, 52).
text.formatted: Public health communications should also make clear the necessity of RCT processes, such as blinding and randomisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52)</ref>.

text.text: Meaningful PPIE and co-production has also been shown to improve trust in study processes in other seldom-reached groups (e.g., autistic adults) (61, 62).
text.formatted: Meaningful PPIE and co-production has also been shown to improve trust in study processes in other seldom-reached groups (e.g., autistic adults) <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(61,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62)</ref>.

text.text: This review is the first to provide a broad picture of the field of RCTs in adults with DS, with the focus on recruitment and retention providing useful strategies for future trials.
We implemented a systematic search, with multiple authors contributing to the search.
We also retrieved studies from a long timeframe, ensuring maximum understanding of the history of RCTs in the DS population.
Although every effort was made to maximise the retrieval of relevant literature, searches may have missed articles not published in English.

The scale of recruitment and retention difficulties is likely under-estimated here due to publication bias in the traditional sense, as well as in the failure of trials to publish target recruitment sample sizes and preregistered protocols, and/or not reporting recruitment and retention strategies utilised.
With the available information, it is not possible to fully capture the 'clinical iceberg' of trials that may have been terminated prematurely due to poor recruitment and retention.
Therefore, the severity of recruitment difficulties outlined here is likely under-reported.
It is also unclear whether some smaller studies may have originally set out to recruit higher numbers, due to a lack of reported target Ns.

This clinical iceberg is further reinforced by our reporting of retention, due to necessary inferences about the number of participants retained as a result of some studies not reporting drop-out rates (i.e., attrition may appear more optimistic than was actually the case; see Table 2).
text.formatted: This clinical iceberg is further reinforced by our reporting of retention, due to necessary inferences about the number of participants retained as a result of some studies not reporting drop-out rates (i.e., attrition may appear more optimistic than was actually the case; see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: In conducting this review it was often difficult to know whether multiple identified papers were reporting on the same trial, with some cases requiring the piecing together of 'clues', such as identical interventions and durations, sample sizes, attrition rates, and numbers allocated to each group, overlapping authorship of manuscripts, etc.
Inadequacies in reporting were also a common feature, with less than a third of trials having been pre-registered, and only a handful pre-publishing a trial protocol.
In addition, the majority of included trials did not report a pre-specified target N nor power calculation.

Given the multifactorial nature of recruitment, encompassing participant-level factors, trial design, and other external factors, recruitment success or difficulty is unlikely to be determined by a single strategy.

If possible, key implementation aspects such as organisational readiness or buy-in should be explored as part of the trial implementation phase (prior to the trial opening) which may further aid recruitment efforts (63, 64).
text.formatted: If possible, key implementation aspects such as organisational readiness or buy-in should be explored as part of the trial implementation phase (prior to the trial opening) which may further aid recruitment efforts <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(63,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64)</ref>.

text.text: Trial teams often apply many recruitment strategies, making it difficult to understand which specific measures are successful.
In addition, understandable priority given to reporting of primary and secondary outcomes may mean that recruitment and retention strategies are under reported in trial publications.
Trial teams should provide comprehensive reports of trial data as per CONSORT guidelines (65), as well as being explicit about the core trial being referred to when multiple papers are published.
text.formatted: Trial teams should provide comprehensive reports of trial data as per CONSORT guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(65)</ref>, as well as being explicit about the core trial being referred to when multiple papers are published.

text.text: Trial teams should consider reporting all recruitment and retention strategies used, their success (actual/estimated), and the contextual facilitators and barriers to participation at an early stage, such as i) working with clinical teams experienced in recruiting adults with DS; ii) integrating PPI, co-production, and qualitative research in the trial to address participation accessibility early; iii) pragmatic inclusion/exclusion criteria based on previous successful studies, exploring if excluding e.g., those with a dementia diagnosis is necessary, or whether a more pragmatic approach such as clinician assessment of capacity to consent can be taken (35); iv) appropriate incentives; v) caregiver concerns, e.g., at the consent stage; and vi) the place where testing and/or follow-up visits take place, including home visits (44).

text.text: Future trials should also consider exploring PPIE and co-production (42).

text.text: When asked about healthcare and research priorities, parents of people with DS most valued research to improve quality of life (67).
text.formatted: When asked about healthcare and research priorities, parents of people with DS most valued research to improve quality of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(67)</ref>.

text.text: Parents also challenge the premise of research into cognitive enhancement (55), preferring research on education, resources, day-to-day support for families, maintaining daily routines, and opportunities for social interaction (68).

text.text: There are some powerful examples of studies involving those with DS as 'authentic co-researchers' and experts by experience, which empowered individuals to contribute in a process they were previously excluded from (69).
text.formatted: There are some powerful examples of studies involving those with DS as 'authentic co-researchers' and experts by experience, which empowered individuals to contribute in a process they were previously excluded from <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(69)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, research must aim to involve people with more severe ID (52), who are generally excluded from RCTs, further entrenching health disparities for this group.
Adults with DS can be facilitated to enrol to and remain in RCTs.

Trial teams should engage people with DS and their carers in meaningful PPI and co-production at an early stage of trial design, as well as involving carers (with participant permission) beyond the consent stage.

Successful strategies to maximise recruitment and retention may include considering whether wider inclusion criteria may be appropriate, minimising study burden, and maximising convenience, e.g., via flexible appointment times and formats, using the shortest suitable intervention duration, and reducing invasive measures.
Research teams should carefully consider the suitability of interventions and outcome measures for their target population and provide support for completing self-report measures.

Retention can also be encouraged by developing a strong therapeutic alliance between trial teams and participants, alongside appropriate incentives, and implementing explorative qualitative work to identify context-specific factors, with the ability to address these sufficiently quickly.

text.text: A standardised extraction proforma was utilised, collecting data about the trial (trial dates, setting, use of blinding, intervention type, control type, number of arms, number of sites), recruitment process (target and actual sample sizes, recruitment strategies, recruitment period), and retention (number of participants completing the primary outcome).
A complete list of extracted variables can be found in Supplemental Material Table 2.
Ten studies from the first search were double-coded by AR to ensure internal consistency, and all studies in the updated search were double coded by JN and AR.
The focus of this review was recruitment and retention rates, rather than outcomes of the RCTs in terms of effectiveness of interventions.
This review therefore focuses on the potential for bias related to lack of statistical power, and attrition bias.
Other risk of bias analyses were not relevant to the study question and so were not assessed.
Quantitative data regarding planned and achieved recruitment and attrition rates are summarised using simple descriptive statistics.
Recruitment rate (%) was calculated, where sufficient data were available, relative to the target sample size as follows: (number of participants recruited / estimated sample size) x100.

Attrition rate (%) was also calculated as the percentage of randomised participants lost to follow-up at the point of primary outcome assessment (6) as follows: (number of participants recruitednumber completing primary outcome)/number of participants recruited.
Where studies did not directly report the number of participants retained to primary outcome, full retention was assumed so as to provide a conservative estimate of attrition.
Information on barriers to and facilitators of recruitment and retention was also extracted and summarised where provided.

Adaptation of the form and support with form completion may have prevented such exclusions.

McGlinchey et al. (2019) co-produced their trial interventions with individuals with DS.

Researchers delivering RCTs with adults with DS should carefully consider their inclusion criteria to avoid over-exclusion, as well as the outcome measures and interventions used, consenting processes, including effective use of legislative frameworks to support participation of those who cannot consent, and involving carers/family where appropriate.

People with DS and their carers can also be meaningfully involved in designing RCTs via Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement (PPIE) and co-production to improve trust in and patient understanding of trial processes, which can in turn improve recruitment and retention.
Trial teams can also aim to maximise convenience and minimise the burdensome aspects of trials.

For example, especially for working-age participants, ensuring flexibility of timings for interventions and appointments, as well as format (remote/home-visit/travel to location), providing person-centred communication including appointment reminders and encouragements, and reimbursing and paying participants appropriately for their travel and time can all go towards improving participation rates.

Measures to minimise participant burden e.g., supporting participants to complete outcome measures, as well as keeping the number and length of outcome measures to a minimum, and limiting the use of invasive measures such as blood tests or reflecting research consensus (35), e.g., in selecting the minimum required invasiveness, (e.g., Diaz et al., 2021; see Figure 2).
